title: India won't sign COP31 electrification pledge or back fossil-fuel phase-out, Yadav says
dek: Ahead of the climate summit in Antalya, the environment minister said India's priorities are climate finance, adaptation and technology transfer, and that the Türkiye-backed '35 by 35' pledge is 'their agenda'.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India will not sign the "35 by 35" global electrification pledge being promoted by Türkiye ahead of the COP31 climate summit, and will not back any roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav has said. The summit opens in Antalya on Monday.

"We are not going to sign any pledge. This is their agenda," Yadav told reporters in New Delhi on Tuesday, according to one report. He said India's formal position would be set out at the conference, which runs from 9 to 20 November. He also said India would not support any plan or roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, citing the government's commitment to providing electricity to its citizens, another report said.

## What India is rejecting

The 35-by-35 pledge was launched in September by Türkiye, which holds the COP31 presidency. It aims to raise electricity's share of the world's final energy use from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035, by electrifying more transport, buildings and industry, one report said.

Separately, Brazil, which presided over last year's COP30 in Belém, has published a voluntary "Roadmap for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Energy Systems". It asks countries to draw up national plans to reduce their dependence on coal, oil and gas, and to build these into their climate pledges and energy plans. It creates no binding targets. COP30 itself did not agree a negotiated roadmap; the Brazilian presidency instead promised two voluntary ones, on fossil fuels and on deforestation.

India has long argued for a "phase-down" rather than a "phase-out" of fossil fuels. Coal still generates most of its electricity. Yadav repeated that position in a media interview in June.

## What India wants from COP31

Yadav said India would pursue "solution-oriented and equitable" climate action and would represent the concerns of developing countries, according to one report. "India has always said that we will be the part of the solution and never the problem," he said, according to another.

According to reports of the briefing, India's priorities are:

- **Climate finance**, which Yadav called "a key priority". He said existing commitments from rich countries fall far short of what developing countries need.
- **Adaptation**: India wants a big increase in funding to help countries cope with climate impacts, and wants the indicators for the Global Goal on Adaptation to stay voluntary and not be tied to access to finance.
- **Technology transfer**, which India says is an obligation of developed countries, along with removing barriers such as high costs, patents and trade restrictions.
- **Common but differentiated responsibilities**, the principle that richer countries, which emitted more historically, should do more. India wants it upheld in full.
- **Carbon markets**, where India says participation must stay voluntary.

Yadav also restated India's opposition to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which puts a charge on the carbon content of some imports into the EU, including steel and aluminium.

India will work with the G77 and China group of developing countries, the Like-Minded Developing Countries and the BASIC group of Brazil, South Africa, India and China, he said.

## Who is going

Yadav will lead India's delegation, with Environment Secretary Narendra Bhooshan and additional secretaries Amandeep Garg and Ashutosh Agnihotri, one report said. Leaders are due to attend a World Leaders' Summit in Antalya on 11 and 12 November. The same report said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is unlikely to attend.

## Why it matters

India is the world's third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases and one of the countries most exposed to climate impacts, from heatwaves to cyclones and floods, including along the Bengal coast and the Sundarbans. Its refusal to back a fossil-fuel phase-out puts it at odds with countries pressing for faster cuts, while its demands on finance and adaptation line it up with other developing economies. The United States, the largest historical emitter, has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement under President Donald Trump.

The negotiations open on 9 November at the Antalya Expo Center.
